note: Sample data only. Shown when no YT_KEY is set. Titles, channels and thumbnails are invented.

items.title: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues, drawn on a grid
items.description: A geometric reading of what an eigenvector actually is: the directions a transformation leaves alone, and the numbers that say how far it stretches them. Worked on a plane first, then in three dimensions.

items.title: Matrix multiplication as the composition of two motions
items.description: Why the row-by-column rule is the only rule that makes composition work, and what the columns of a matrix are telling you about where the basis vectors land.

items.title: The four fundamental subspaces, and why they fit together
items.description: Column space, null space, row space and left null space, with the dimension bookkeeping that links them. Includes rank-nullity and a short argument for why the pairs are orthogonal.

items.title: Singular value decomposition from first principles
items.description: Every matrix is a rotation, a stretch, and another rotation. Building the SVD out of that sentence, then using it to compress an image.

items.title: SN1 and SN2: the two substitution pathways side by side
items.description: Rate laws, stereochemistry and the solvent effects that decide which mechanism wins. Drawn on a chalkboard, step by step, with the transition states shown.

items.title: Carbonyl chemistry: nucleophilic addition and its reversals
items.description: Why the carbonyl carbon is electrophilic, how the tetrahedral intermediate forms, and the conditions that send the reaction back the other way.

items.title: Aromaticity and Hückel's rule, without the hand-waving
items.description: Counting pi electrons properly, and why the 4n+2 rule falls out of the orbital picture rather than being a rule to memorise.

items.title: Hypothesis testing and what a p-value is not
items.description: The logic of the null model, the sampling distribution, and the three claims a p-value cannot support. Ends with a small simulation you can run yourself.

items.title: Maximum likelihood, explained with one curve
items.description: Start with a likelihood, take a log, set the derivative to zero. The whole method on a single parameter, then a note on why the log matters.

items.title: The central limit theorem, demonstrated rather than asserted
items.description: Repeated sampling from a deliberately lopsided distribution, with the running histogram converging on a bell. Discussion of the sample sizes where it still misleads.
